To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adaptation measures are deployed in ways that correlate with specific metrics of risk exposure and socioeconomic markers, and that adaptation measures are interconnected.

(1) adaptation decisions are made relative to metrics of risk and socioeconomic factors; (2) shoreline armoring correlates to higher levels of socioeconomic development and lower levels of racial diversity; (3) property acquisitions correlate with lower levels of socioeconomic development, higher levels of racial diversity, and low levels of armored coastline; (4) nourishment is only used in areas with armoring and is not correlated with critical infrastructure; and (5) the use of different adaptation measures is interconnected.

shoreline armoring is deployed disproportionately in high-income, high-density communities with low racial diversity; property acquisition is deployed disproportionately in low-income, low-density communities with high racial diversity; and beach nourishment is deployed exclusively in communities with shoreline armoring.
